nameStory: The yellowtail damselfish gets its name from the bright yellow tail fin that stands out like a sunny beacon against its otherwise brownish body. The 'damselfish' part of the name comes from these fish being considered delicate and beautiful, like a maiden or damsel, though they're actually quite feisty and territorial despite their pretty appearance.
description: The yellowtail damselfish is a small, colorful tropical fish that's normally found in warm Caribbean waters but has been spotted once in New England waters. Adults have brownish bodies with a distinctive bright yellow tail fin, while young fish look completely different with violet bodies decorated with blue spots and clear fins. These fish are typically small, reef-dwelling species that prefer warm, coral-rich environments.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Adults display a striking contrast between their dull brown body and brilliant yellow tail fin that catches light like a golden flag underwater

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, oval-shaped body that feels firm and muscular when handled, typical of the sturdy damselfish family

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small fish that would fit comfortably in your palm, with a deep body that's taller than it is long

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single dorsal fin runs along most of the back, with the tail fin being distinctly separate and fan-shaped

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Typically found near rocky structures or artificial reefs in warm water, often hovering close to shelter they can dart into quickly

habitat: In New England waters, this would be an extremely rare vagrant visitor, likely brought north by warm Gulf Stream currents during unusually warm periods. Any sighting would probably occur in deeper offshore waters or around artificial structures like oil platforms where water temperatures remain warmer longer.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be present as waters are still cold from winter, well below the tropical temperatures this species requires.
seasonality.summer: The only season when a vagrant individual might possibly survive briefly in New England's warmest surface waters during heat waves.
seasonality.fall: Any summer vagrant would likely perish as water temperatures begin dropping below tropical levels.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent as New England waters are far too cold for this tropical species to survive.

funFact: Young yellowtail damselfish look so completely different from adults - with purple bodies and blue spots instead of brown with yellow tails - that scientists originally thought they were two separate species entirely!
confusionNotes: In New England waters, any small tropical fish with a yellow tail would be so unusual that confusion with native species is unlikely. However, other tropical vagrants or escaped aquarium fish might cause identification challenges.
contextualKnowledge: This fish's presence in New England would be so extraordinary that any sighting should be carefully documented and reported to marine biologists, as it would represent a significant range extension likely related to climate change or unusual ocean currents.
compareHints: As the only Microspathodon species in the dataset, compare it to other damselfish family members by looking for the distinctive yellow tail fin that sets it apart. Most other damselfish in northern waters would be different vagrant tropical species, but none would have this specific brown body and bright yellow tail combination.
